text:
Maya: quick RFC follow-up — we need to pick an approach for on‑prem bundle manifests. Do we use a signed transitive dependency graph (nodes reference digest IDs of child nodes) or a flat top‑level index that lists blobs (content‑addressed)? I think a graph makes partial apply and parallel fetch easier, but it pushes more responsibility into the operator. opinions?

Ethan: graph = nicer for resume and delta apply. operator must be able to validate graph integrity and GC unreachable nodes though. otherwise you get dangling blobs in offline caches.

Priya: flat index is simpler for operator reconciliation (CR status maps directly to top‑level manifest). but it can be huge for big images and forces whole revalidate on any change. also makes partial apply awkward.

Leo: middle ground idea: top‑level index that references signed, content‑addressed subgraphs (shards). each shard is a small transitive graph. operator only has to understand shard boundaries for apply/resume. reduces GC and validation blast radius.

Maya: that hybrid sounds promising. sketch of a shard header: 
```yaml
shard_root: sha256:abcd...
signed_by: ops-key-v1
entries: [manifest-1, manifest-2]
```
The shard root is signed once and covers all entries. then the operator verifies shard signatures and streams blobs.

Ethan: streaming verify is key for airgapped installs. operator should verify signature as bytes arrive rather than download whole blob then validate. avoids doubling storage.

Priya: question: who verifies transitive signatures? operator or verifier agent on node? in high‑security setups we prefer node‑side verification so the control plane never sees unverified content. but that adds CPU burden to nodes.

Leo: operator can do signature envelope checks and a lightweight manifest sanity check; full crypto verification (and key / HSM checks) happen on node at activation. operator exposes an API to request a verification receipt from node that says "I validated shard X and applied Y".

Maya: sounds like split responsibility. operator: shard orchestration, partial fetch, lifecycle; node: final crypto attestation + activation. that also lets operator GC based on node receipts.

Ethan: rollback story — we should use time‑limited activation leases. node gets an activation token signed by operator with TTL. if activation fails or service reports bad health, node can auto‑revert before TTL expiry. avoid global hard rollback pivots.

Priya: implementation note: activation lease fields: 
```yaml
activation_token: <sig>
issued_at: 2026-03-21T15:00:00Z
ttl_seconds: 3600
fallback_manifest: sha256:ffff... # optional
```
Operator rotates lease signing keys; nodes accept leases tied to operator key ID.

OpsBot: deploy-bot: can add metrics: shard_fetch_time, verification_latency, activation_failures. log correlation id = <shard_root>. :chart_with_upwards_trend:

Maya: one more tradeoff — verifying full transitive chain on operator simplifies centralized attestation for enterprise customers (they want one audit trail). but it increases memory/io on operator in constrained airgap gateway. maybe make full‑chain verify an opt‑in enterprise flag.

Leo: agreed. default = operator envelope + node attest. enterprise opt‑in = operator full verify + stored verification receipts.

Ethan: security nit: use a Merkle root over blob contents in shard rather than simple list so we can do partial proofs for individual chunks. makes streaming verify easier.

Maya: action items: I'll draft an RFC addendum with the hybrid shard approach, streaming merkle verify, activation lease model, and operator/node responsibility matrix. @Priya can you write a short operator API sketch for receipts? @Leo can you prototype a shard header format and merkle layout?

Priya: yep — will drop an API sketch this week.

Leo: I'll prototype header + small CLI tool to build shards.

Maya: thanks all :thumbsup: 

(OpsBot reaction: :rocket:)
